rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: It is said that God called to Moses from a tree in the valley.
rows.anchor: It is said that in the valley God called to Moses from a tree (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: The tree is identified as a kind of lycium or boxthorn (ʿawsaj) plant.
rows.anchor: that was a kind of lycium or boxthorn (ʿawsaj

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the referent to be the tree from which God called Moses.
rows.anchor: It thus refers to the tree (JJ) or, alternately,

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭ, Bg, R
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies it with the fire Moses saw, which consumed the tree.
rows.anchor: to the fire that Moses perceived (see v. 10; IK, R, Ṭ) and which consumed the tree (Bg, R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One report says Moses was told to remove his sandals because they were made from the skin of a dead donkey.
rows.anchor: either because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Removing the sandals is explained as reverence for sacred space, as people remove shoes before entering the Kaʿbah sanctuary or any mosque.
rows.anchor: out of reverence (taʿẓīm

rows.speaker: al-Ghazzālī
rows.claim: Al-Ghazzālī reads the command as casting aside attachment to both this world and the next, turning wholly toward God.
rows.anchor: al-Ghazzālīsuggests that in being asked to remove his sandals Moses was being instructed to cast aside this world and the next world

rows.speaker: My, Qu
rows.claim: Sufis take the phrase to mean that the heart should be free of attachment to both worlds and devoted solely to God.
rows.anchor: for Sufis the verse means that one’s heart should be free of any attachment to the things to be found in this world

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah glosses the phrase as leaving the two realms of existence to witness the Presence of the Existentiator.
rows.anchor: As Ibn ʿAjībah explains it, the phrase means,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sandals became a recurrent Sufi image and symbol in poetry and inspired literary works, including Ibn Qasī’s book Taking Off the Sandals.
rows.anchor: has inspired a number of artful literary works in Islamic civilization, such as the book Taking Off the Sandals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A famous poem attributed to Ibn ʿArabī explains the Divine intent as relinquishing both worlds and removing the veils between.
rows.anchor: In a famous poem attributed to Ibn ʿArabī, the Divine intent behind the imagery is explained:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭuwā derives from a root meaning “to fold up” or “to become enwrapped.”
rows.anchor: the name of the holy valley in which Moses encounters God is Ṭuwā, which comes from a root that means “to fold up”

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: The valley symbolizes the inner holy sanctuary and Ocean of Divine Presence, where existence is folded up and Moses’ soul is enwrapped in Divine Reality.
rows.anchor: the inner, holy sanctuary that symbolizes the Ocean of the Divine Presence above all states of existence (Aj)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God’s choosing Moses means conferring messengerhood and the special distinction of direct address, hence his title Kalīm Allāh.
rows.anchor: addressed by God directly (R)

rows.speaker: Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī
rows.claim: Al-Dārānī says God found Moses’ heart the most humble among Adam’s children and therefore singled him out for direct speech.
rows.anchor: According to the early Sufi figure Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This command is identical to 79:17, parallels the wording in 20:43, and is linked to other Moses narratives.
rows.anchor: This verse is identical to 79:17 (cf. v. 43); see also 26:10–11; 27:12; 28:32

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to both Moses and Aaron echoes the command to Moses in 20:24 and is linked with 79:17 and other Moses passages.
rows.anchor: Cf. the similar wording addressed to Moses in v. 24; 79:17; see also 26:10–11; 27:12; 28:32

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Z
rows.claim: Some commentators connect the gentle address with the invitation in 79:18–19 to be purified and guided to the Lord.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, the command here is similar to the words God tells Moses to speak to Pharaoh in 79:18–19

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: “Gently” may mean “a gentle word,” understood by some as the shahādah, “There is no god but God.”
rows.anchor: lā ilāha illa’Llāh; IK). Gently

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The command can be taken generally as requiring Moses to communicate God’s message to Pharaoh gently.
rows.anchor: Gently is also seen as a general command to Moses to communicate the message to Pharaoh in a gentle manner (IK)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that harsh admonition makes tyrants more obstinate and proud, whereas gentleness might let Pharaoh respond positively.
rows.anchor: it is customary for tyrants, when they are admonished harshly, to increase in their obstinacy and pride

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Since Pharaoh raised Moses, al-Rāzī says gentleness was fitting in recognition of caregivers’ rights.
rows.anchor: since Moses was brought up by Pharaoh, it was only fitting that Moses be gentle with him

rows.speaker: JJ, IK
rows.claim: “Remember” means to heed Pharaoh’s warning or to turn away from his misguidance.
rows.anchor: Remember here refers to Pharaoh’s taking heed of the warning given to him (JJ) and turning away from his misguidance (IK)

rows.speaker: JJ, IK
rows.claim: “Fear” means that Pharaoh would fear God and return to Him, or become obedient to Him.
rows.anchor: fear is understood to mean that Pharaoh would be fearful of God, return to Him (JJ), and be obedient toward Him (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laʿalla conveys “perhaps,” “hopefully,” or “it might be that.”
rows.anchor: “perhaps,” “hopefully,”or “it might be that”

rows.speaker: JJ, R
rows.claim: The hopeful “perhaps” is for Moses and Aaron, who cannot know the result of their warning but are to hope Pharaoh will heed it or fear God.
rows.anchor: haply is said for the benefit of Moses and Aaron (JJ), who could not know the outcome of delivering God’s warning

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Their fear that Pharaoh would act hastily is understood as fear that he would hasten their punishment; his swift execution of the sorcerers illustrates this tendency.
rows.anchor: refers to his hastening their punishment (JJ); for Pharaoh’s tendency to punish swiftly as evidenced by his summary execution of the sorcerers

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, Moses and Aaron feared Pharaoh would kill them before considering the proofs they brought.
rows.anchor: it can refer to Pharaoh’s killing them without actually pondering over the proofs they would have brought to him (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Their fear of Pharaoh’s transgression can mean that he would exceed bounds in punishing them.
rows.anchor: the concern that he would go beyond bounds in punishing them

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, they feared that Pharaoh’s disbelief would increase as he tried to refute them.

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: God’s assurance that He is with them means that He will protect and help Moses and Aaron.
rows.anchor: God’s telling Moses and Aaron that He is with them is understood to mean that He will protect them and help them (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Moses and Aaron invited Pharaoh to believe in God and release the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh and his people controlled.
rows.anchor: Moses and Aaron were inviting Pharaoh to believe in God and to free the children of Israel (Kl) who were under the control of Pharaoh

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Pharaoh killed Israelite children, forced the people into labor to serve him, and humiliated them.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh used to kill their children and force them into labor in order to serve him, all the while humiliating them (Kl)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: The singular “a sign” collectively refers to Moses’ miracles of the staff and the white hand.
rows.anchor: A sign from your Lord is a collective reference to the miracles of Moses’ staff and his white hand (Kl)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Those who believe God’s signs receive peace from God, angels, and believers, bringing safety in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: whoever believes in God’s signs will have greetings of peace from God, the angels, and the believers

words: أَنَّ ٱلْعَذَابَ عَلَىٰ مَن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ
rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The denier who turns away from God’s signs will face punishment in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: punishment in this world and the next shall come upon him who denies God’s signs and turns away (Aj)

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: “All Our signs” refers to the nine signs Moses brought to Pharaoh and his people.
rows.anchor: Our signs, all of them refers to the nine signs that Moses brought to Pharaoh and his people (JJ, Z)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Pharaoh denied the signs and refused to accept the truth.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh denied the signs and refused to accept the truth (Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: “Sorcery like it” means sorcery like the kind Moses had brought.
rows.anchor: Sorcery like it means “sorcery” like the kind that Moses had come with (Ṭū)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary points to similar sorcery accusations made against Moses, Jesus, Muhammad, and other prophets.
rows.anchor: For references to similar accusations of sorcery made against Moses, Jesus, Muhammad, and other prophets

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: A tryst refers to the fixed time set for the meeting.
rows.anchor: A tryst and neutral place refer to the fixed time of their meeting (Ṭū)

rows.speaker: M
rows.claim: The neutral place refers to the location of the meeting.
rows.anchor: and its location respectively (M)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ staff devoured the sorcerers’ deceptions, exposing their work as false.
rows.anchor: When Moses cast his staff, it devoured all their deceptions (7:117) and whatsoever they did was shown to be false (7:118)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ statement parallels his declaration in 10:77 about the ultimate futility of sorcery.
rows.anchor: See also 10:77, where Moses makes a similar statement about the ultimate futility of the work of sorcerers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After their defeat the sorcerers turned back humbled; the commentary also points to 20:89.
rows.anchor: After the sorcerers were defeated, they turned back, humbled (7:119). See also 20:89c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the sorcerers’ prostration and declaration of faith, the commentary directs readers to 7:119–22.
rows.anchor: See commentary on 7:119–22.

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: The sorcerers’ certainty in God made them see worldly trials and pleasures as fleeting and finite beside eternal felicity in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The sorcerers reached such a high degree of certainty in God that they came to see the trials and pleasures of this life as merely passing

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: God’s rewards exceed Pharaoh’s rewards, and God’s punishment, when meted out, lasts longer than Pharaoh’s punishment.
rows.anchor: the rewards that God can give are better than the rewards that Pharaoh can give, and that God’s Punishment, when meted out, is more lasting

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage is cross-referenced with 7:123–26 and, for verse 71, 26:49.
rows.anchor: See commentary on 7:123–26; cf. also v. 71 with 26:49

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: While Moses was on the mountain, God informed him that the people had gone astray; he returned angry and grieved.
rows.anchor: While on the mountain, Moses was informed by God that his people had gone astray. He thus returned to them in a state of anger and grief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing the Israelites worship the idol, Moses threw down the Tablets in anger and shock.
rows.anchor: when he saw their worship of the idol, he threw down the Tablets in anger and shock

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Moses had left Aaron in charge, he rebuked him for what happened during his absence.
rows.anchor: Since Moses had left Aaron in charge of the Israelites, upon his return he rebuked Aaron for what had happened while he was absent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is admonished not to covet worldly goods given to the Makkans who reject him.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is being admonished not to desire the things of the world that have been given to the Makkans who are rejecting him

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: “That We may test them concerning it” means that God will punish them for it in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: That We may test them concerning it means “that We may punish them in the Afterlife on account of it” (Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: The provision is the Hereafter’s reward promised to the Prophet, better and more enduring than the disbelievers’ worldly enjoyments; the passage parallels God being called better and more lasting.
rows.anchor: the rewards that God has promised the Prophet in the Hereafter are far better and longer lasting than the enjoyments He has given the disbelievers in this life

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Spiritually, God’s provision refers to trust in Him (tawakkul), more enduring than one’s own efforts to obtain what one wants.
rows.anchor:
out the things one
wants (Su)

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Alternatively, provision refers to contentment with God together with complete reliance upon Him.
rows.anchor: Alternatively, provision here could be a reference to both contentment with God and total reliance upon Him (Su)

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: One view takes “family” (ahl) to mean the Prophet’s close relatives.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another view takes ahl to mean the people of the Prophet’s faith, hence “thy people”; ahl can mean either family or people.
rows.anchor: while others say that it refers to the people of his faith (R), in which case thy family would be rendered “thy people” instead

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Although the command addresses the Prophet, it applies to believers generally.
rows.anchor: Although this injunction is addressed to the Prophet, it applies to the believers in general (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assurance that God provides is compared with 51:57–58, where God says He seeks no provision from people.
rows.anchor: We ask no provision of thee; We provide for thee is similar to 51:57–58

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The end belonging to reverence means that Paradise is for the reverent.
rows.anchor: the end belongs to reverence means that Paradise is for those who are reverent (see 2:2c; JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Qurʾānic passages also say that the end belongs to the reverent.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere in the Quran, it also says that the end belongs to the reverent (7:128; 11:49; 28:83)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The opening verse of al-Anbiyāʾ announces that the time of reckoning is approaching.
rows.anchor: The first verse of al-Anbiyāʾ announces that the time of the reckoning approaches (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥisāb denotes the accounting of the Day of Judgment, also called the Day of Reckoning.
rows.anchor: is a word used to signify the accounting of the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: some theologians (Q, Z)
rows.claim: Some theologians say more time has passed since creation than remains until the world’s end.
rows.anchor: Some theologians have said that the time that has passed since God created the world is greater

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The chronological argument rests on iqtaraba ordinarily indicating that one is closer to one’s destination than one’s origin.

rows.speaker: M
rows.claim: From God’s perspective reckoning is near in relation to His knowledge, not temporally, since He knows all moments simultaneously; humans think it distant.
rows.anchor: from God’s point of view the reckoning is close—not in a temporal sense, because God knows all moments simultaneously—but rather is close with regard to His Knowledge

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Commentators say each person’s certain death is reason enough to regard reckoning as near, regardless of when the world ends.
rows.anchor: part of what is signified by their reckoning draws nigh (Q)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Q
rows.claim: Being heedless means caring only for this world and paying no attention to the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: To be heedless means that people only care about this world (Ṭ) and pay no attention to the matters of the Hereafter (Q)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Sufis distinguish those heedless through worldly engrossment from righteous believers mindful of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: there are those who are heedless of the Hereafter because they are engrossed in worldly affairs, and there are the righteous believers who are mindful

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Another kind of heedlessness arises from being so absorbed in remembrance of God that one gives no thought to the Garden or Fire.
rows.anchor: there are also those who are heedless of the Hereafter because they are so engrossed in the remembrance of God that they give no thought to the Garden

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The claim that God has a child can refer to Quraysh’s belief that angels are God’s daughters.
rows.anchor: the reference is to either the belief among the idolatrous Quraysh that the angels were “daughters of God”

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, the claim can refer to the Christian doctrine of Jesus’ Divine sonship.
rows.anchor: or the Christian doctrine of the Divine sonship of Jesus (see, e.g., 4:171c)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say the verse was revealed specifically about Khuzāʿah, who regarded angels as God’s daughters and worshipped them for intercession.
rows.anchor: According to some, this verse was revealed specifically in connection with the tribe of Khuzāʿah, who considered the angels to be daughters of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Khuzāʿah interpretation, the “honored servants” are the angels.
rows.anchor: honored servants refers to these angels

rows.speaker: some Muslim theologians
rows.claim: Some Muslim theologians allow calling God “Father” in a narrow metaphorical or symbolic sense.
rows.anchor: Some Muslim theologians do not object to calling God “Father” in a narrow metaphorical or symbolic sense

rows.speaker: some Muslim theologians
rows.claim: They reject offspring understood as unlike other creatures in ontological status because they were begotten by God, or exclusive sectarian claims of divine filiation; 5:18 answers that people are created mortals whom God may forgive or punish.
rows.anchor: consider it erroneous to assert that any such Divine “offspring” are not like other creatures and would have a different ontological status by virtue of being begotten by God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The emergence of Gog and Magog signals that the end of the world is approaching.
rows.anchor: The coming of Gog and Magog is a sign of the impending end of the world (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: “The true promise” refers to the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: The true promise refers to the Day of Resurrection (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The second phrase may alternatively be read, “The stare of those who disbelieved will be fixed.”
rows.anchor: The second phrase of this verse could also be read to mean, “The stare of those who disbelieved will be fixed” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Their fixed stare results from fear in the face of the terrifying event.
rows.anchor: which will occur because of the fear they experience in the face of this horrible event (Q, Ṭ)

words: قَدْ كُنَّا فِى غَفْلَةٍۢ مِّنْ هَٰذَا
rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ confession of heedlessness reflects their inattention to these matters during worldly life.
rows.anchor: We have certainly been heedless of this reflects the fact that in the life of the world they paid no attention to such matters (R)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Symbolically, Gog and Magog are the preoccupations, tumult, and impressions that assault and corrupt the soul and expose it to satanic influence.
rows.anchor: Gog and Magog represent, at the level of spiritual symbolism, the preoccupations, tumult, and impressions that assault the soul
